analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from tightening ozone air pollution limits until most violators comply.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on S. 751: it sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee after one hearing and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the EPA from issuing a stricter ground-level ozone (smog) standard until at least 85% of counties currently violating the existing standard came into compliance. It also would have required the EPA to designate a county as violating only on the basis of direct air monitoring rather than modeling, to weigh feasibility and cost when setting the standard, and to publish at least one analysis that leaves out health benefits from cutting pollutants other than ozone.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries facing expensive emission controls under a tighter ozone standard — power plants, refineries, manufacturers, and other operations in counties near the current limits — benefit if the bill passes. The bill delays or softens the compliance burden and shrinks the number of counties subject to it by requiring designations based only on direct monitoring.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from finalizing any ozone standard lower than the one in effect on January 1, 2015, until at least 85% of counties in nonattainment areas have achieved full compliance with that standard.
Restricts the EPA to designating counties as violating the ozone standard only on the basis of direct air quality monitoring, rather than modeling, which would shrink the map of regulated areas.
Requires the EPA to take feasibility and cost into consideration when setting the ozone standard, contrary to the Clean Air Act's traditional focus on health alone.
Requires at least one regulatory impact analysis for the rule that excludes any benefits from reducing pollutants other than ozone, which would understate the rule's total measured benefits.

analysis.who_pays: People living in areas with unhealthy ozone levels — especially children, the elderly, and people with asthma and other respiratory conditions — would wait longer for cleaner air. The health costs of delayed or weaker standards fall on the public while the compliance savings accrue to polluting facilities.

drawbacks.text: Delaying a tighter ozone standard leaves residents of high-ozone areas exposed to smog linked to asthma attacks and respiratory illness for years longer than current law would allow.
Counting only ozone-specific benefits in the required analysis would understate the real health gains of the rule, since cutting ozone-forming emissions also reduces other harmful pollutants.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that designating violating counties only by direct monitoring could leave counties with modeled violations off the regulated map, shifting the compliance burden to counties that do monitor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades avoided compliance costs for a small set of energy and manufacturing industries against longer exposure to unhealthy air for people in violating counties. Its accounting provisions would make the rule look less beneficial than it is by excluding co-benefits, so the weighing is skewed toward the regulated industries' costs and away from the public's health gains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got a single hearing in June 2015, was never voted out of committee or brought to the floor, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the Clean Air, Strong Economies (CASE) Act in the Senate on March 17, 2015, with 22 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The bill attracted 27 cosponsors — 26 Republicans and one Democrat, Joe Manchin of West Virginia.
The Environment and Public Works Committee held a hearing on the bill on June 3, 2015 (printed as S.Hrg. 114-47), but the committee never voted to report the bill to the Senate floor.
No further action occurred after the hearing, and the bill expired with the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017, without a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA kept its existing authority to set stricter ozone health standards, and people in areas with high ozone levels kept the prospect of tighter protections. The power plants, refineries, and manufacturers the bill would have shielded got no relief from compliance costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public health rules stayed intact; industry got no relief

for.name: John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors; it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

for.name: 26 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Majority Leader and the Environment and Public Works chairman.

for.name: Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democrat among its 27 cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill in June 2015 but never voted it out of committee or scheduled a markup, leaving it without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican: 26 of the Senate's 54 Republicans cosponsored, joined by a single Democrat (Joe Manchin), and the bill never reached a roll-call vote.

industries.note: These facilities are the largest sources of ozone-forming emissions and face the biggest control-equipment costs under a tighter standard. The bill would delay or weaken that standard, shifting the cost of dirtier air onto nearby residents.

A lower ozone standard would put more counties out of compliance and subject factories there to stricter permitting and controls. The bill's compliance milestone and monitoring-only designation rule would shrink that burden, at the public's expense in air quality.

Emissions from drilling and production contribute to ground-level ozone; delaying a stricter standard postpones controls on these operations. The one Democrat cosponsor, Manchin of West Virginia, represents a coal- and gas-producing state, reflecting the fossil-fuel lean of the coalition.
